I wrote a small Python program called BAPD which is a GUI environment to be able to write, compile and run Bally Astrocade assembler programs. It is currently in the first Alpha release but I wanted to make it available just to see if it is of interest to anyone. You can find it here:

https://github.com/TinyMouse42/BAPD/releases/tag/v1.0.0

Check the README.md for a description and simple installation instructions.
I haven't wrote any operating documentation yet but it is pretty intuitive to use.
The program comes with a default project containing the source for the Bally Demo program which is ready to compile and run.
It's probably not something for the heavy hitters (you know who you are - LOL) but if you just want to play around with assembler programming this greatly simplifies things.
It has a few annoying bugs. For example, when it opens MAME, it opens a black command window while MAME is running. It doesn't hurt anything but is is annoying to me.
Feedback that doesn't involve throwing tomatoes at me is encouraged. I don't even know if this is something that would be useful to anyone. If it is, I'll continue to develop it.

*It is Non-Invasive:* The BAPD program is designed to be non-invasive and self-contained. It will not make any changes to your computer beyond creating a dedicated "BAPD" directory under your user profile directory. All of the program's files and data will be stored within this BAPD directory, ensuring that it does not interfere with or modify anything else on your system.

Long ago, Bob Colbert shared the ballybin and astrowav source code, but it wouldn't compile on modern compilers. I probably could have figured it out with sufficient effort, but I never put much effort into it. I figured I would see if ChatGPT could help with setting up a project and fixing the errors and warnings, and this is exactly the sort of boilerplate work it excels at. So, here is ballybin and astrowav 1.4.1. I haven't tried to add any functionality, but this has everything set up if anyone does want to try to enhance it. There is also a ballybin 2.0, but while some of the new features are cool, I never got as much success in actually processing recordings with that version.

I set this up in Visual Studio Code, which is a free IDE from Microsoft. There will probably be some setup required if you haven't used it before. Download the program here:

https://code.visualstudio.com/

Install some extensions--

* Open Visual Studio Code and go to the Extensions view ( Ctrl+Shift+X ).
* Install the following extensions:

* *C/C++* (by Microsoft): Provides C++ IntelliSense, debugging, and code browsing.
* *CMake Tools* (optional, but recommended if you use CMake).
* *Code Runner* (optional): Allows you to run code snippets or files with a simple click.

Install the g++ compiler--

* 

*Step 1: Download and Install MSYS2*

* Download the installer from https://www.msys2.org/
* Follow the installation instructions.

* 

*Step 2: Update the Package Database and Install GCC*

* Open the MSYS2 terminal (search for "MSYS2 MSYS" in the Start Menu).
* Update the package database and core system packages:
pacman -Syu

After the terminal restarts, update again if prompted, then install the toolchain:
pacman -S mingw-w64-x86_64-toolchain

* 

* This installs g++ along with other essential tools.

* 

*Step 3: Add MSYS2 to System Path (Optional)*

* You can add the MSYS2 mingw64/bin directory to your PATH environment variable if you want to use g++ directly from the Windows Command Prompt.
* The path typically looks like C:\msys64\mingw64\bin.

* 

*Step 4: Verify Installation*

* Open a new MSYS2 MinGW 64-bit terminal and type g++ --version.

To compile the programs, open the project workspace ballybin1.4 source.code-workspace and compile through the menu or control-shift-b.

Regarding the viewer, the 32 pages of hues are derived from the most significant 5 bits of the color byte, which represent the hue. This encoding allows for 32 distinct hues. 21866:
I uploaded a video called "Showing All 256 Colors of a Real Bally Arcade/Astrocade" to YouTube today.  You can view it here:

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Auxwy8oos1Q

I created this video to help show the difference between the 256 colors displayed in the MAME emulator versus the colors displayed on a real Astrocade game console with an RF-output connected to a CRT TV.  I did have some have trouble capturing exactly what the TV was displaying.  Perhaps in the future someone can create a similar video with direct-video capture using an Astrocade that has been modified for composite or s-video output.  This would allow a clearer picture with more exact colors to be captured and used for color reference.

I show the range of the Astrocade's 256 colors using several different programs, including:

1) "256 Color Display" by Jerry Burianyk (1981)
2) "Color Pick 2 (with Hex Output)" by Lance Squire (2011)
3) "Color Viewer & Color Matcher" by Ryland Dagger (August 2024)
4) "Color Wheel" by Dick Ainsworth (1978) - From the Bally BASIC manual
5) "Standard Color Generator" by Andy Guevara (May/June 1981)

All of these programs, both the cartridges and AstroBASIC programs, were loaded from the BackBit Pro cartridge.  The BackBit Pro is a universal instant-loading cartridge that plugs into the 50-pin expansion on the back of the Astrocade.  It is capable of interfacing with a multitude of vintage computers and game consoles via proprietary adapters.  Program images are loaded from a microSD card inserted into the cartridge.  You can learn more about this useful cartridge for vintage consoles and computers, here:

https://www.youtube.com/eviesrevue

For those who are unfamiliar with the system, I give a bit of background about the Astrocade, including a close-up of the motherboard.  I narrate the entire video to try to help keep it interesting.  For a bit of fun toward the end of the video, I show a few dozen pictures that were converted by "Bally Image Works," by Chris Martin.  These are four-color pictures displayed in a resolution of about 160x102.

Video Notes:

In this video, I show the colors of a real Bally Arcade/Astrocade game console.  I took this video using a Canon PowerShot SX60 HS camera setup on a tripod.  The camera was pointed at a 14" Toshiba color television.  This flatscreen CRT TV is a model 14AF45 that was manufactured in November 2005.

At 1 1/2 hours long, this video probably isn't for everyone.  I aimed to please those hoping to get a better color reference of what the colors look like on a real Astrocade.  Yet, I tried to make it enjoyable for the casual classic video game fan too.  I'm not sure if I found the right mix, but I tried my best.

Enjoy!

21877:
Yesterday, on October 13, 2024, "tahrey" left extensive comments for my "Showing All 256 Colors of a Real Bally Arcade/Astrocade" video. This person made some excellent points that are of benefit to this thread.  I would hate to see the extensive ideas put into these comments not be seen by other Astrocade fans just because the ideas end up buried in the comments section of my YouTube video.

As a reminder, there is a link to me "Showing All 256 Colors of a Real Bally Arcade/Astrocade" video in this thread:

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Auxwy8oos1Q

Here are "tahrey's" three comments about the video:

---------- Comment 1 ----------

Writing on my phone whilst watching on my TV... Some thoughts -

First, easiest method of extracting proper colour codes by the general method you're thinking of... Get a DVD recorder, if you don't have one around anywhere. Throw a disc in, set it to highest quality, tune in to the console. Connect the TV through composite or component or Svideo... Whatever. Check that the colours still look OK. Start the recording and step through that first program that showed eight colours at a time with maybe 2 - 3 seconds per page (DVD standard recording has keyframes about every half second so that should be more than enough). Finalise the disc and put it in a computer, run a player that can do screenshots like VLC, make sure colour corrections are all neutral and things look as expected. Do a grab of each page, then sample the bars in a paint package. Maybe use an adjustable blur filter to do a long vertical smear but only average two to four pixels horizontally, and take your samples from the centre of each bar.

Should be a lot less work and a lot more accurate and reliable a result. The colour accuracy of modern devices like DVDRs is generally pretty good and doesn't suffer the same kind of drift that old analogue TVs and VCRs did, and the colour depth of DVD recording is greater than both the console and typical PCs. There's also a set formula for converting between the internal YUV colour space and computer RGB, though there's two slightly different methods (depending on whether you limit the contrast to give some wiggle room for calculation errors with certain colour extremes, or clamp it to the maximum range of RGB and accept little clipping in exchange for better contrast - for your purposes you might want to take the average of those if you have the ability to switch).

Also, given that, an even simpler method is... If the YBR colour values the video chip produces are known, then you should be able to convert those to at least the idealised RGB equivalents using the same formula, same as is used for the C64, C16, Atari 8-bit etc palettes. The difference here of course is if the analogue factors in output from the vid chip, transmission to the modulator, then whatever processing that may do and how things may drift in its own output might affect the final values.

This is where some kind of cheap scope may help, you could just probe those individual lines coming off the video chip and see what voltage levels each colour equates to, using that basic program which changes the entire screen including the borders (maybe make it so the code in the top left can be turned on and off?). After all if you do an output mod that skips the RF stage of the modulator (composite, Svid) or the entire modulator itself (component), the result should be functionally the same. Might even be able to do that with a plain multimeter, normalising the numbers to the actual reported black and white (plus pure colours which give max/min Cr and Cb) values vs what would be expected (as the blanking and sync areas of each frame will bias the average a bit)...?

As for what's going on with the camera, if you Vl [... comment cut short, possibly due to lenth]

---------- Comment 2 ----------

Ok something glitched there... Anyway if you want to persist with this way of doing it, there's a few things i think may be the main problems at this point and are hopefully easy to address if your camera is flexible enough to allow manual white balance -

1. The moire effect from it being high rez enough to pick up the individual pixel stripes but not enough to avoid interference patterns... Turn the video resolution way down, or maybe switch to stills and see how low / high you can go and if one or other will fix it (though high rez will bring in the extra problem of having to average out the RGB sub pixels). Alternatively, or maybe in addition... Enable manual focus, or whatever mode may allow you to force it to focus on some object temporarily held halfway between TV and camera, and deliberately DEFOCUS it. So long as you have reasonably defined bars (or even entire screen...) and some suggestion of which code each one is, you don't need pin sharp images, and there was a moment partway through the video where it autofocussed on your hand instead of the screen and the bars looked SO much better with that little bit of smoothing. Also may help to zoom OUT then crop the images down afterwards. Even a final size of 160x100 is probably overkill TBH...

2. The exposure and blowing-out... It's giving me vibes of a very typical digital camera issue (especially the more mass consumer market ones) where the contrast and colour saturation is preset way too strong, which gives a nice vibrancy to casual snapshots, but is terrible for colour accuracy and preserving detail in shadows and highlights, ie no good for any serious photography or calibration.

Something that I've ended up having to do with a lot of cameras in the past (only now not needing to do it as much with my prosumer grade Sony RX100, which has RAW mode and a less extreme default profile) is using whatever built in image adjustments are on offer to back those off, often to the absolute minimum it allows, which tends to give a fairly natural and accurate result instead of being at all washed out or monochrome.

If that Canon shares anything with the A720 I used to have, then that'll give a pretty perfect result for those particular aspects. However, still be best to tune it specifically so the viewfinder pic looks as close to the TV as you can get it. Might not need to mess with the white balance beyond what you've already done, then.

(oh, almost forgot - the third aspect of the vibrant snapshot tuning is that the image tends to be both over sharpened and subject to excessive noise reduction... The latter might actually be preferable here, but the former needs to be reduced as far towards "soft" as possible in general, or at least a notch or two below the default... May help reduce moire even without defocus and resolution reduction, but it's also just better for general photos a lot of the time, not to mention compression efficiency)

The other part would probably be stopping down the exposure a bit, it's maybe a bit too bright. Probably having SOME ambient light in the room would help, but make it very soft and indirect. Like, use an adjustable LED lamp that you can tune to have the same "white" tone as the TV does, and a brightness around that of medium grey (or brighter so the TV bezel is about the same as the medium grey colours) and located so it doesn't reflect off the screen.

Again, that's something the camera should very much allow. If nothing else there should be a general exposure adjustment where you can nudge it lighter or darker, but I'd expect it to have more manual options so you can change the actual exposure time and aperture. In this case the camera doesn't seem to be quite synchronised with the TV all the time, so it's maybe trying for 1/60th second but they're not entirely in agreement over how long that is, so there's an occasional moving band that shows the scanning beam and phosphor decay. Likely be better to push that out to 1/30th, 20th, even 15th sec (using slow shutter mode for video if you have that) and closing the aperture down quite a bit to compensate and reduce how much light gets into the camera. Pushing the ISO to the minimum (100 or less if available) will also help with that, and improve colour accuracy and noise into the bargain.

And lock these off if at all possible - calibrate the settings combination to what seems good, then make sure it can't be automatically "improved" by the camera's firmware which very definitely isn't programmed for this. May be helpful to turn on all the display info overlays, get close to it with semi automatic modes, then switch to full manual mode and transfer those figures over to it for final tuning. Then they should stay static throughout the run and not end up varying up and down and causing problems in the pursuit of "optimising" and balancing each shot, when you're trying to capture information that very much isn't balanced.

Hopefully combining those (saturation, contrast, defocus/reduced resolution, reduced light input but longer exposure, etc) should help make the colours more even and accurate, and particularly help with those red pages where many of the colours looked the same but for a few dark moire bands. I know it sounds like a lot of work, but it doesn't really take long to adjust each individual item and in the main they shouldn't really have domino effects that you then end up chasing after in a never ending circle. Like, drop the ISO as far as possible, lock the exposure to something that's a multiple of 1/60th, then all you have to do to adjust image brightness is tweak the aperture. Set the saturation, contrast, sharpness to minimum and only turn them up if it seems like one or other has gone too far. Flip to manual focus and move it a little so the moire disappears but colour bands are still discernable. Reduce the image resolution. And... That's the bulk of it already done.

... I'm sure i had a 3 as well, but i forgor. Maybe it got incorporated into the above?

(oh and... Even with lowered resolution, make sure your compression quality is set to extra fine or whatever it's called on your camera. And remember you might want to normalise the colours in the final images if it turns out you crushed the ranges a little too far... The actual colour depth we're dealing with means it can stand not being full 24 bit range to start with, and you can always expand back up from a crushed range but not recover the lost information from too much contrast)

I suppose if you wanted to get really fancy you could get a standard colour calibration sheet and dial the camera into that using the light from the TV showing an all white image... But by that point you may as well just get the vector scope. Or borrow a DVD recorder and a USB optical drive for the PC.

---------- Comment 3 ----------

NB at some points it looks rather like the TV itself may not be in entirely pristine condition... Like I'm not sure if it's actually just a fringe effect of the moire, but it looks like it has some freckles of inconsistent colour, particularly in the mid-upper area on the right hand side. Bit of phosphor burn that's not noticeable under normal use conditions. That may not help much, though i think the bars don't reach too far into that area.

If that's the case then probably best to get 256 individual shots of the full screen colour swatches, crop down to remove the worst area plus the code number, then apply a very strong blur filter over the cropped image so you can get the overall average colour by sampling the dead centre?

----------

The Astrocade's sound is part of the system's I/O chip and is called the "Music Processor."  Do you have any controller issues (try checking all of the controllers, including controllers 3 and 4)?  A full description of that chip is here in the "Nutting Manual:"

21882:
The first thing I would try is replacing the modulator with a known good one. That's the last stage before the TV. If that don't work, it would probably be the I/O chip. It's the one closest to the on/off switch. Tho only other part that could go bad is R32 (a 1K 1/4 watt resistor closest to the power in connection)  brown -black-red color rings. There could also be a bad solder joint on the resistor. last but not least, the pins that connect to the modulator mat need cleaning. A pencil eraser does that job very well.If all of that fails, the last part of the equation is the on-board ROM. It interprets the sound codes.  Please let us know what you find.Thanks, Ken Lill

https://ballyalley.com/ml/ml_docs/ml_docs.html#NuttingManual
There are several folks here who can probably point out non-I/O-chip issues that could affect the sound of your Astrocade console, Ian.  I hope that you're able to get your console's awesome sound effects and music working again.

21886:
Hi, Ian,    The ONLY chip that should have a heat sink on it should be the DATA chip. Putting heatsinks on the others just makes it hard to know which chip is which if you happen to remove more than one at a time and the other 2 don't usually get hot enough for a heatsink.If you have, or can get, a container of "freeze spray", that will help diagnose what is heating up and causing the problems. when it "blacks out" or goes crazy, just spray a little on one chip or component at a time. When it comes back to Ife, you have probably solved the problem! I would start with the DATA chip because they are the hottest usually. Then I would go to the I/O next.If you can't find the problem, Allen usually can!

21895:
like I said before, several times here do NOT glue any heatsinks on the custom I/O or ADDRESS chips. Later, if you happen to take them off, you won't be able to tell one chip from another. If you look at the schematic, you will see that the power points are on different pins. Putting them into the wrong socket could cause more problems than ever. With the capacitors being so old they could explode or catch on fire. I really do not recommend gluing anything on the I/O or ADDRESS chips. The only kind of heatsink that you can use there is the clip-on type.

On November 10, 2024, James Marienthal wrote, "Wasn't the cooling factor the major downfall of this console [the Bally Arcade/Astrocade]? That’s why chips failed? Or am I wrong"

The early Bally Professional Arcade (BPA) certainly had chips (mainly the Data chip) that failed early on in its life in 1978 due to overheating problems.  Some of these issues were fixed to a large extent in different versions of the Bally Arcade with variations to the RF shielding, including using the shielding as a heat sink.  I don't think that the overheating issues ever were extinguished entirely, but by the time the Astrocade was released by Astrovision, Inc. (soon-after: Astrocade, Inc.), overheating was less of a problem due to, as I understand it, reduced voltage to the Data chip.

Dan Koppen wrote a short how-to article called "Krazy Koppen's Heat Sink" in the June 8, 1981 issue of the "Arcadian" newsletter that shows how to reduce the voltage to the Data chip, which, I think, was standard on the Astrocade.  You can read the short article here:

https://www.ballyalley.com/newsletters/arcadian/arcadian_vol_3/arcadian_vol_03_issue_08.pdf#page=5

As for the overheating of the custom chips being the downfall of the Bally Arcade: no, I don't think this is the case.

The "Arcadian" and "Cursor/BASIC Express" newsletters are a great source of information about why the Bally Arcade failed in the marketplace.  If I remember correctly, Bally opened their Atlantic City casino in New Jersey in late 1979.  I believe that Bally stopped production of the game system in 1979 to focus all of their resources and funds on that casino.  The BPA system was up for sale through-out part of 1979/1980.  At least one company (I can't remember who right now), not Astrovision, Inc., were close to purchasing the BPA, but the sale fell through at the last moment, which delayed the reintroduction into the marketplace of the BPA.

The BPA was unavailable for quite some time, maybe a year (according to what I've read in the newsletters).  Having been out of production for all or most of 1980, the system wasn't available again until its re-release in 1981.  Then it became widely available and even got a great push and a second wind with widespread positive coverage in "Electronic Games" magazine in the early 1980s.

In a way, rather than a failed system, I look at the Bally Arcade/Astrocade as one that was quite successful, though in a minor fashion.  It was able to weather the storm of its troubled beginning.  It usurped the simple cartridge-only plans for the system and had a version of BASIC released for it that created a homegrown community that carried on through the newsletters into the mid-eighties.

Does the Bally stand on the same turf as the Atari VCS?  Certainly not.  How about the Intellivision?  Nope.  Or the Odyssey 2?  Perhaps.  And yet.  And yet... what?

People loved their Bally Arcade/Astrocade systems.  If you look at BallyAlley.com, then you'll see that hundreds of games were made for it (mostly in BASIC).  Many people bought the Bally Arcade as a game console, then got Bally BASIC and the tape interface and discovered that they had actually bought a low-cost computer.  The Astrocade even shipped with Bally BASIC/AstroBASIC, so that those who had purchased it had a computer out-of-the-box. It all depends on how you define success. It certainly was long-lived (~5 -
6 years) relative to other consoles (=success), but, using the
Odyssey2/VideoPac (1978 - 1984) as an example, is known and used by far
fewer people today (=not a success; plus the O2/VP was released and
relatively popular in multiple territories with at least a modest amount of
mainstream third party support). It's a bit like the Intellivision in that
regard. Sure, the Intellivision technically was on the market from 1979 -
1990 (=success), but it really wasn't a competitive platform after 1984
(=just long-lived). Similarly, when can we say the Astrocade was genuinely
competitive? Probably up to maybe 1980 - 1981? That's only a couple of
years it was a viable option for those in the market for a video game
console. Otherwise, it just served a specific niche consumer like the
Intellivision from 1985 - 1990.

In any case, like many other platforms, the fact we're still actively using
it, and talking about it, is an undeniable win. There's nothing wrong with
being in a second or third tier of consoles. Some platforms didn't even

21911:
From a commercial standpoint it was a pretty big flop. Bally offloaded it because the system sold in the tens of thousands in 78-79, and while that was a real lull for home gaming in general Atari was up to roughly 1 million units sold overall by the end of 79, and as far as I am aware the Channel F and Odyssey2 were selling through all their manufactured units.  Obviously the QC issues and delays were a major factor, but there's also the price tag - the BPA cost something like 300 bucks new, putting it way more expensive than the $150~ price range other consoles were targeting. It's cheap for a computer, but the full expansion never actually came out, making it a very awkward computer indeed. Astrovision did all right with it in 81 but even by the bankruptcy they had only sold in the low hundred thousands.
Technologically it's head and shoulders above everything else up until the ColecoVision and Commodore 64 debuted in 1982, and its indie development community is absolutely unlike anything else in the home market save for like.. Famicom BASIC in Japan. And if that's your metric, it's a success! It's a success in terms of good arcade ports and having unique, cool games, too! Of all the failed systems of the 70s and early 80s it's probably my favorite, but I can't pretend it wasn't a cursed piece of kit for folks trying to make money off it.

"Head and shoulders above everything else" prior to ColecoVision (or, we
can more generally say, the 1982 console releases (I wouldn't include
computers, as there's really no fair way to compare it to something like
the TI-99/4 or Atari 8-bits, which were far more expensive)) is a strong
statement. It was definitely better than the likes of the Faichild VES, RCA
Studio II, Coleco Telstar Arcade, APF M/MP-1000, Interton VC4000, and
Odyssey2 . I'd say the Atari 2600 had faster processing and pushed more
colors. The Intellivision had more colors and, arguably, a better
processor, though it's debatable whether it was a better processor for
gaming. Areas where the Astrocade excelled certainly were base RAM, 4K
versus usually 1K or less (even the ColecoVision had only 1K RAM), which
did/does/could make a difference. So, personally, I'd be more comfortable
in saying that the Astrocade was easily technologically competitive
(acknowledging every platform has some pluses and minuses) from launch
(1978) through 1982, and, from a technology standpoint, was certainly near
the top in many areas. Almost four years at or near the top consoles
technology-wise isn't bad, even then. I'd certainly agree that if it were
marketed and distributed better, and had far more enticing games and games
of high quality, it could have been quite the contender.

21914:
There are only 8 wires in the joystick. 1 is the common for the 4 switches that control the x - y motions of the controller. Pin 8 is the common. Pin 1 has no contact inside the connector, there is no wire there.the other wires are:2) Down3) Left4) Right5) Trigger 6) UP7 and 9 are connected to the pot (Knob)
There is no set pattern for the colors. I have seen many variations. If wire 1is broken the pot will still work, but none of the switches will.I 7 or 9 are broken, the pot won't work. all other wires go to the individual x -y positions. If all wires have continuity, then it's probably the I/O chip.

21915:
This is your best guide:
Bally Hand Control (9-Pin Layout)

Sounds like a broken common wire (yellow).Hold the stick in any direction and move the wire coming out of the bottom of the controller in a circular pattern or back and forth kind of slowly.  Don't be afraid to move it too far, because your wire is probably already broken.If you have an Ulti-Multi, set your switches to 1100 0111 (TESTS) and press 4 for hand control tests while doing this.  If you get an arrow to flash in any direction then you have a broken wire.Take the controller apart (6 screws).  Cut the wire above the "protector" where it comes out of the bottom of the hand controller.  Cut the wire about an inch below it as well.  You will remove about 2-3 inches of cord total.  Check for continuity with the yellow wire and the plug to make sure you removed enough.  Strip all 8 wires on both sides, get some small heat shrink tubing, solder the wires back together and "seal" the heat shrink.  Make sure you put the heat shrink tubing on before you solder the wires back together.  Split the "protector" length wise with an exacto knife.  Most pull off with some needle nosed pliers, starting with the smaller/bottom end.  Put it back on when the repair is done, and snug up a zip tie to the cord inside the controller to keep the cord from pulling out.  If you get really good at this, it's about a repair that can be done in about 30 minutes (more if you clean the pot while you're in there), but it's painful and tedious unless you're in the mood.Or just buy these:  Bally Astrocade controllers - LOT OF 4 - PLEASE READ! | eBay

Apologies for the necro bump of this old thread, but I think it is worthy of a bump.  I was playing around with Hot Rod Bally Basic in the MAME debugger today to see if I could figure out how to get it working, even though I really don't know Z80 assembler very well.  I loaded HRBB from AstroBASIC in the debugger (hey, I see the names of Ken Lill and Leroy Flamm in HRBB!) and used the debugger to disassemble the code to a text file. I noticed this little snippet of code in the disassembly:

7BD7: DB E1       in   a,($E1)
7BD9: E6 02       and  $02
7BDB: C8          ret  z
7BDC: DB E0       in   a,($E0)
7BDE: E6 7F       and  $7F
7BE0: FE 20       cp   $20
7BE2: 30 10       jr   nc,$7BF4
7BE4: 4F          ld   c,a
7BE5: 06 00       ld   b,$00
7BE7: 21 09 7C    ld   hl,$7C09
7BEA: 09          add  hl,bc
7BEB: 7E          ld   a,(hl)
7BEC: A7          and  a
7BED: 20 05       jr   nz,$7BF4
7BEF: 3C          inc  a
7BF0: 32 81 8C    ld   ($8C81),a
7BF3: C9          ret

I was intrigued by the reads from the mysterious input ports $E1 and $E0, and also by the fact that the result of IN a,($E0) was ANDed with $7F, which just happens to be the ASCII code for the SCROLL keyword that HRBB kept repeatedly printing.  In MAME's debugger, I changed the $7F to $7A, and reset the emulated machine with F3.  When you do a reset in the debugger, AstroBASIC is restarted, but the contents of RAM where HRBB resides are not cleared.  I did a CALL 24576 to re-launch HRBB, and lo and behold it now repeatedly printed the POINT keyword instead of the SCROLL keyword.  Intriguing!  I then, like a total pro, decided to crudely NOP the entirety of the code from 7BDC to 7BF2, leaving the RET to return from the subroutine, reset, did a CALL 24576, and whaddya know, HRBB actually worked.  So I have uploaded the patched version of HRBB to my GitHub repository at https://github.com/tonymokonen/Astrocade for your enjoyment.

What the heck are those ports?  I noticed similar IN statements from these ports in Blue Ram Basic, but when I set a breakpoint on them, BRB never seemed to execute them.  It's almost as if that code was a vestigial remnant from the original HRBB.

Edit:  When I say "it works", I mean that it runs a Hello World type program just fine.  I haven't fully tested all commands.  It does support :INPUT for 300 baud cassette format in MAME, but I don't think it has any support for 2000 baud.

21942:
I’ve been working on assembly code for the Astrocade and wanted to share a few pitfalls I’ve come across. Hopefully, this will be helpful to others working on similar projects. If you have any workarounds, tips, or insights, I’d love to hear them.

· *GETNUM Issue:* The GETNUM function is missing a mask, causing it to malfunction with single digit entry when using alternative fonts or enabling zero suppression.

· *STRDIS Alignment Problem:* STRDIS does not display text correctly if the background differs from the screen background and the X coordinate is not perfectly aligned to avoid any shift.

· *VBLANK Overwrite:* VBLANK requires an additional horizontal byte to the right of the pattern, which can overwrite adjacent graphics in that byte.

· *PLOP Overwrite:* A similar overwrite issue occurs when writing patterns with PLOP.

· *Math Function Requirements:* Some mathematical functions require 11 BCD bytes to operate correctly.

· *Interrupt Handling After PAWS:* When using reentrant code with an ISR, you must disable interrupts after calling PAWS to prevent conflicts.

· *MUZCPU Crashes:* I experienced crashes in the MUZCPU instruction set when working with the built-in calls, jumps and loops.

· *MAME Color Palette Discrepancy:* The MAME color palette does not accurately match the actual hardware.

· *Alphanumeric Control Code Differences:* Control codes for alphanumeric displays behave differently on hardware compared to MAME. Hardware requires hex values, while MAME also accepts the corresponding ASCII characters.

· *Magic Register Pixel Shifting:* When shifting pixels with the magic register, you may need to write zero to the "waster" after finishing to clear any pixels shifted out of the last byte you wrote to.

I'm glad you're experimenting with ChatGPT more, Adam. That definitely helps to get an idea of its strengths and weaknesses. It's a very alien intelligence, and yet it is intelligent by any useful definition of the term. Whether or not there's anything *there* in terms of subjective experience, I'm not even sure how we'd answer, but you can't help but get that sense sometimes interacting with advanced language models. I don't know if the critics haven't used it enough, only used the very early versions (it's much improved over just the last two years), or just don't want to believe it's useful.

Which model are you using? If you can use the full o1 model (as opposed to o1-mini, 4o, etc.), it's quite good at programming because it can think through its answer in the background before responding to you. (There are at least more message limits with free plans.) Of course it's not flawless 100% of the time, but given that it's not even running the programs (yet), that's hardly surprising. I have to guide it along, but I've written usable code with it and it's used libraries I wasn't even familiar with that would have taken me quite some time to research before.

Astrocade programming will be tricky because the base model hasn't been trained on copious Astrocade BASIC code (though it no doubt does understand QBASIC). I did try to have it write an Astrocade program long ago, but it couldn't really get the specifics of the Astrocade BASIC variant. However, the newer models are more intelligent and have a much longer context window, so I wouldn't rule it out. You can give o1 quite a long prompt--many program examples, maybe even the complete Astrocade BASIC manual if you had it in text format. (I wish some of the infrastructure were a little better. Why can't I just upload a large image .pdf?) If you really wanted to get working programs, that would be the direction to go. And they're already announced their next model (o3), which when given enough compute can solve visual puzzles designed to be difficult for computers, solve Ph.D. level math problems, and compete in coding competitions at a grandmaster level.

There are several free OCR (Optical Character Recognition) software tools available that can help you convert scanned documents or images into editable text. Here are some popular options:
1. Tesseract OCR

  *   Overview: Tesseract is one of the most accurate and powerful open-source OCR engines available. It can recognize text from images and is widely used in various OCR applications.
  *   Pros:
     *   Highly accurate text recognition.
     *   Supports many languages.
     *   Works well with both printed and handwritten text (though the latter may require additional training).
     *   Can be integrated into various software for custom OCR solutions.
  *   Cons:
     *   Requires some technical setup (especially for beginners).
     *   Can be complex to use via command-line, though GUIs are available.
  *   Download: Tesseract OCR<https://github.com/tesseract-ocr/tesseract>

2. FreeOCR

  *   Overview: FreeOCR is a Windows-based software that uses the Tesseract engine. It's straightforward and has an easy-to-use interface.
  *   Pros:
     *   Simple interface, good for beginners.
     *   Fast and accurate, especially for English-language text.
  *   Cons:
     *   Limited support for languages other than English.
     *   The user interface is a bit outdated.
  *   Download: FreeOCR<https://www.paperfile.net/>

3. Capture2Text

  *   Overview: Capture2Text is a lightweight OCR software that allows you to extract text from any part of your screen. It's simple and runs directly from the Windows tray.
  *   Pros:
     *   Portable (doesn't require installation).
     *   Easy to use for quick text extraction.
     *   Supports multiple languages.
  *   Cons:
     *   Only works with image files (no PDFs or document processing).
  *   Download: Capture2Text

4. OnlineOCR.net

  *   Overview: If you don't want to download and install any software, OnlineOCR.net is a free online OCR service that allows you to upload an image or PDF and extract text directly through your browser.
  *   Pros:
     *   No installation required.
     *   Supports PDF and image files.
     *   Free tier for basic usage (with some limitations).
  *   Cons:
     *   Limited to a few pages per conversion in the free version.
     *   Less control over the OCR process compared to local tools.
  *   Website: OnlineOCR.net<https://www.onlineocr.net/>

5. Google Drive (Built-in OCR)

  *   Overview: Google Drive provides a free OCR feature when you upload a scanned document (PDF or image) to Google Drive. It can automatically recognize and extract text from images in Google Docs.
  *   Pros:
     *   No software installation needed (web-based).
     *   Automatically detects text from images.
     *   Easy to use and works well for documents stored in Google Drive.
  *   Cons:
     *   Limited accuracy with complex formatting or handwritten text.
  *   How to Use:
     *   Upload your image to Google Drive.
     *   Right-click the image and select Open with > Google Docs.
     *   The text will appear in a new Google Docs file.

6. SimpleOCR

  *   Overview: SimpleOCR is another free OCR software that can be used for both scanned documents and handwritten text (though its handwriting recognition is limited).
  *   Pros:
     *   Simple and easy to use.
     *   Free for personal use.
  *   Cons:
     *   Limited accuracy with handwritten text.
     *   The free version has some feature restrictions.

Conclusion:
If you're looking for a powerful and free solution, Tesseract OCR is highly recommended, especially if you're comfortable with a bit of technical setup. Game Instructions from the "Cursor" newsletter:

Here are the rules for Hamurabi. After you answer each question press 'GO'

1.  At the start a person needs 10 bushels of grain per year to live. Farm worker strikes can change this. They may accept up to 2 less bushels than they demand. If your offer is rejected there will be no harvest. Strike amount equals 10 plus your settlement.

2.  55% of the people must be fed or your term of office may expire.

3.  You may buy or sell land at prices from 17 to 26 bushels per acre.

4.  It takes 3 bushels to plant an acre and 1 worker to plant 10 acres.

5.  Term of office is twenty years. If you can make it.

NOTE: It would help to have a calculator close at hand if you want to win!

Hamurabi: Story and Gameplay Summary

Background/Story Summary: "Hamurabi" is a strategic resource management game where you assume the role of a ruler governing an ancient Sumerian city. Your task is to ensure the survival and prosperity of your people over a twenty-year reign. Inspired by the historical figure Hammurabi, the game challenges you to balance the delicate interplay of land, grain, and population while dealing with unpredictable events such as plagues, strikes, and natural disasters.

As king, your performance will be evaluated based on how well you feed your population, grow the city, and manage resources. Failing to meet the people's needs or mismanaging resources may lead to starvation, strikes, or even your removal from office. Success requires careful planning and adaptation to the unexpected.

Key Elements of the Game:

* Feed your people with available grain.
* Buy or sell land to optimize resources.
* Plant crops to harvest grain for future years.
* Navigate disasters such as rat infestations, droughts, and plagues.
* Maintain enough food to prevent strikes and ensure the population's survival.

Victory Conditions:

Successfully complete your twenty-year reign with a healthy population and strong resource management. If you fail to provide for your people, you may face impeachment, exile, or worse.

  *   R: Bushels lost to rats.
  *   S: People who starved in the current year.
  *   T: Bushels stolen by thieves.
  *   U: Acres sold in a transaction.
  *   V: Input for the player's name.
  *   W: Strike flag (1 if a strike occurs, 0 otherwise).
  *   X: Counter for name input and string processing.
  *   Y: Year counter in the main game loop.

Two-Letter Variables

  *   NT: Note time, used to adjust game speed.
  *   TV: Temporary variable for displaying player name in GOSUB 360.
